transcript: The other day, I saw Counting and Cracking at the NYU Skirball Center. Presented here by The Public, this huge play is making its North American premiere with a cast of 19, a run time of three and a half hours, and a family story spanning decades. The starting point for us as the audience is somewhat through the lens of one of the primary characters named Siddartha, who's been completely assimilated into Australia since his mother moved there from Sri Lanka during her pregnancy. There’s much he doesn't really know about his family's recent history, and pretty much the rest of the play is spent laying that all out. We see how a family's personal circumstances intertwine with political contexts, in this case bringing some devastating consequences. It’s hard to really explain just how vast the scope this play is — it's moving, it's funny, it's historical, it's deeply theatrical with its live underscoring, live translations, and live sound effects created using Foley. I think the expansiveness and depth of this piece makes it quite universal because everyone's family has its own Homeric history whose significance can best be understood by those who've been through a part of it. This play affords just the privilege of seeing such a comprehensive account and the ripple effect of single moments for generations. It’s a long piece but its length is very earned and it doesn't drag at all, so if you're thinking about going do not let the run time deter you. Counting and Cracking is running through September 22nd at the Skirball Center. With that, another program for my collection.
